candidates.prune_reason: Lumbar radiculopathy — Absent right distal pulses, elevation‑worse plantar pain, and exertional calf claudication in the setting of heavy smoking and diabetes strongly indicate ischemia; these vascular findings and symptom pattern are not consistent with S1 radiculopathy.

differential_evidence.description: Local foot/ankle examination: positive Tinel sign over the tarsal tunnel (medial malleolus/posterior tibial nerve) or reproduction of plantar paresthesia with direct compression — supports tarsal tunnel vs vascular or radicular causes.

Vascular signs and tests: diminished/absent distal pulses, cool/pale foot on elevation, delayed capillary refill, abnormal ABI (<0.9) or low toe pressures — support PAD/ischemia and argue against isolated entrapment or pure radiculopathy.

Neurodynamic and spine signs: positive straight leg raise or slump test reproducing plantar symptoms, plus focal neurologic deficits in S1 distribution (reduced Achilles reflex, S1 sensory loss, or motor weakness e.g., plantarflexion weakness) — supports S1 radiculopathy.

Electrophysiology and distribution pattern on testing: Nerve conduction study showing focal tibial nerve slowing across the tarsal tunnel (local entrapment) versus diffuse sensory nerve action potential reductions consistent with peripheral (length‑dependent) neuropathy, versus EMG findings of radicular denervation in proximal myotomes (favoring radiculopathy).
